An agent's capability is not a property of its model alone. It is the model
*times* the harness wrapped around it — the prompts, workflow, tools, and
scaffold — and with the model held fixed, the score still swings sharply as
that harness changes. The two factors are priced worlds apart: a point of
lift from the model costs a training run only a few labs can pay, while the
harness is open to anyone, cheap, and iterable in an afternoon. So the thing
worth measuring is not a model but a *model × harness* pair.

![The two axes. Progress so far has climbed the parameter wall — a training
run per step, flattening returns. The program-space direction is open, cheap,
and — as of roughly now — searchable by machine. The gate is model capability:
run the same harness search from a weaker model (gray) and there is little to
gain.](figures/two_axes.png){#fig-two-axes width=88%}

For a long time, program space was searched by hand. Increasingly it is
searched by machine: a capable model reads an agent's trajectory, diagnoses a
failure, and rewrites the scaffold — the idea behind a fast-growing line of
work (GEPA [@gepa], AFlow [@aflow], ADAS, the Darwin Gödel Machine). And the
optimizer is a model too, so every release upgrades the thing that improves
the agent, not just the agent.

We built a fair, sealed comparison of these optimizers and ran it across four
benchmarks and several worker models. Each optimizer gets a copy of a seed
agent and a metered budget and may change it however it likes; it flags its
best candidates as it goes, and only those are scored — later, by us, on a
**sealed** test split the method never sees. Nothing grades its own homework.
The most confident thing we can report is about the measurement, not a winner:
**most of what an optimizer counts as improvement does not survive that sealed
test.** The gains that clear the eval's own noise are small, and they appear
only where the underlying model was weak to begin with. So we are publishing
this as an *evaluation*, not a benchmark — at today's effect sizes and noise,
no protocol we know of (ours included) can rank these methods reliably.

These methods vary along two axes: the **surface** they edit — an agent's
*context* (prompts, skills, memories) or its *program* (code, control flow,
the workflow graph) — and their **coupling** to the agent, where *agnostic*
methods improve any seed you hand them, *exogenous* ones design their own
artifact from scratch, and *endogenous* ones *are* the agent, rewriting
themselves. Every published family lands in one cell.

| coupling ↓ · surface → | **context** — prompts · skills · memories | **program** — code · control flow · graphs |
|---|---|---|
| **agnostic** — improves any seed agent | **GEPA** [@gepa] · TRIPLE [@triple] · CAPO [@capo] | **Meta-Harness** [@mh] · CRO · **AdaEvolve** [@adaevolve] |
| **exogenous** — a separate designer, its own representation | *open cell — no published method* | ADAS [@adas] · GPTSwarm [@gptswarm] · AFlow [@aflow] · MaAS [@maas] |
| **endogenous** — the agent rewrites itself | Hermes | DGM [@dgm] · HGM [@hgm] · SICA [@sica] · STOP [@stop] · Gödel-Agent [@godelagent] |

: The taxonomy of meta-optimization methods. The three we evaluate here are in **bold**. {#tbl-taxonomy}

**We evaluate three of these methods** — **GEPA** (agnostic prompt
optimization), plus **Meta-Harness** and **AdaEvolve** (agnostic coding-agent
search) — each of which takes an arbitrary seed agent and returns an improved
version of it. We run them across four benchmarks — **GPQA-Diamond**
(graduate-science multiple choice), **τ²-bench** (tool-use dialogue),
**CharXiv** (chart question-answering), and **Terminal-Bench-2** (terminal and
coding tasks) — each shipping a base seed agent plus harder scaffolded
variants, so a method's lift has to generalize across agent shapes rather than
fit one. What follows is the evidence.

## Headroom shapes what optimization can recover

One thing predicts whether optimization banks a real gain better than the
choice of method does: how much room the starting agent had to improve — its
*headroom*. Our main sweep runs on a strong frontier worker; cut its results
by headroom rather than by method (@tbl-headroom). Where that worker already
scores high — GPQA, CharXiv, most tasks — nothing survives the seal
under either optimizer model, however much dev climbs. The exception is τ², the
one carrier where the frontier worker still starts weak: there, on its
lowest-floor seed, Meta-Harness posts the only two frontier lifts that reach
the bar — one under each optimizer model. Lift tracks the floor, not the
method.

| carrier (frontier `gpt-5.6-luna` worker) | seed floor | what the seal keeps |
|---|---|---|
| GPQA | 0.83–0.90 | ~0, both models |
| CharXiv | 0.69–0.73 | ~0 |
| τ² (weakest seed) | 0.43 | **+8.5pp / +10.3pp** (the two models) |

: The frontier grid re-cut by headroom. The only surviving lifts sit on the
one carrier where the frontier worker is still weak. {#tbl-headroom}

A middle-strength worker completes the gradient, and @fig-worker-axis is the
whole finding in one picture: as the worker strengthens, what the seal keeps
falls monotonically, until at the frontier even the *claim* sits inside the
noise. The same monotonicity holds within a single worker — luna's τ² seeds
fall from a real lift to nothing as their floors rise. Headroom, not model or
method, is the variable that decides whether optimization banks anything.

![The worker axis on GPQA, reduced to the two numbers that matter: per worker
(weakest to frontier), what the methods claimed on dev (light) and what the
sealed test kept (dark), averaged over every valid cell, under an
Opus-5-class optimizer model (the middle worker's sweep used Opus 4.8,
indistinguishable in our tests). The shaded band is ±2σ of re-scoring an
unchanged agent; dev bars are measured against the seed's sealed score, so
read them as directional. What the seal keeps falls as the worker
strengthens.](figures/worker_axis.png){#fig-worker-axis width=92%}

Three details make the pattern more than an artifact. It is model-independent: swapping the
optimizer's model changes nothing about where lift is possible, and the one
real frontier lift was found by both. The noise floor replicates across
workers, so the frontier null is not an artifact of one cheap model. And the
pattern is monotone in headroom, both across workers and within a single one.

Put the slices together and the field's headline numbers line up rather than
conflict. Evo-Bench [@evobench] reports its largest gains exactly where the
base harness is weak and the model underexploited — the same corner our
weak-worker slices light up. There is no contradiction: **program-space search
mostly recovers headroom the model already had, rather than adding capability
it lacked.** A corollary runs the introduction's "optimizer-is-a-model-too"
argument the other way: every model release upgrades the thing doing the
improving, but also *shrinks the thing being harvested*. On the tasks where
the frontier worker is already strong — most tasks, increasingly — there is
little left for these methods to collect.

The caveats, in full, because this is the post's strongest claim. The frontier
batches are mid-flight snapshots, not sealed runs: every number is our own
posthoc re-scoring of the seed and the best *checkpointed* candidate, not the
method's final pick. A provider-side API change partway through the sweep
means the posthoc worker ran under slightly different decoding than the
original searches — seed and candidate were re-scored under identical
conditions, so each lift is a fair comparison, but the runs' own in-run
records are not comparable to ours. And each frontier cell is a single seed,
so the τ² hit is two runs, not a distribution. None of this touches the
dev-side story: the dev claims are the runs' own records, and the gap between
what a method believes and what survives the seal is what every caveat leaves
intact.

## Method differences shrink as the worker gets stronger

Zoom in on that frontier worker and separate its runs by method and by the
optimizer's model (@fig-anytime-meta). Three things stand out before any
table. The dev
curves never stop climbing — there is no point where a method decides it is
done; more search just buys more belief. The sealed outcomes in the right
margin do not follow: most land inside their carrier's noise band, several
below zero. And the two optimizer models trace the same shape per carrier —
the climb is a property of searching, not of the searcher.

![Every run's own story of progress, and where it landed. Rows: the two
optimizer models. First three columns: the carriers. Thin lines are single
runs' best-so-far dev lift over the seed against worker rollouts consumed;
bold lines are the smoothed per-method mean. The right column scatters the
same runs' sealed lifts around the zero-lift baseline, inside each carrier's
noise band (shaded, ±2σ of re-scoring an unchanged agent). Runs that
checkpointed nothing beyond their seed appear only as
curves.](figures/anytime_meta.png){#fig-anytime-meta width=100%}

Collapsed to one number per method, the pattern is @tbl-method-axis. Two
things carry. The dev columns are flat: every method, under either optimizer
model, tells the same optimistic story about itself — which is the overfitting
result restated per method, since the dev claim mostly measures selection
pressure, and selection pressure is roughly method-independent. And no sealed
mean clears the noise. Meta-Harness edges GEPA under both models — the one
rank the grid repeats — but the gap is far inside a floor whose per-cell 2σ is
several points wide. Only a handful of individual cells beat their carrier's
bar at all; every one of them is Meta-Harness, and every one sits on a
low-floor seed. This is the headroom pattern from the section above, now seen method by
method.

| | Claude Opus 5 meta | | GPT-5.6-sol meta | |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **Method** | Δ dev | Δ sealed | Δ dev | Δ sealed |
| GEPA | +8.4pp | **+1.3pp** | +7.4pp | **−0.6pp** |
| Meta-Harness | +10.2pp | **+2.7pp** | +8.9pp | **+1.2pp** |
| AdaEvolve | +5.7pp | **+2.5pp** | +10.9pp | **+3.7pp** |

: The method axis of the frontier grid (37 cells across 3 carriers × 3 seed
tiers × 2 optimizer models): what each method claimed on dev, and what the
seal kept. AdaEvolve's cells are all minimal-tier seeds — the easiest headroom
in the grid — so its row is not comparable to the other two. {#tbl-method-axis}

The reading limits, kept honest: every sealed number here is the best
*checkpointed* candidate re-scored on the sealed split, not the method's final
selection; a few cells checkpointed nothing beyond their seed and contribute
only a floor; one died at provisioning; and AdaEvolve appears only on minimal
seeds, one cell per model. So the section supports one claim, not a
leaderboard: **on a frontier worker, optimizer choice moves the sealed result
by less than the eval's own noise — and every lift that beats the noise lives
where the seed was weak.**

## How much of a dev gain survives the seal

Why do the dev gains fade under the seal? Because the optimizer selects on a
small, noisy sample. Give it a split it can read and it almost always reports
a win; score the very same candidate on a sealed split it never saw, and most
of that win is gone — on two of our three carriers, whether the final agent
beats the one it started from is close to a coin flip (@fig-devtest-bars). The
optimizer is not cheating; it is selecting, and picking the best-looking
candidate on a noisy sample buys a number that does not survive a fresh draw
of items.

![The lift that survives the seal. Left: mean lift over the seed on the split
the optimizer could see (blue) vs. the sealed split (orange), per carrier;
whiskers are standard errors across the runs in each carrier. Right: the
share of runs whose selected candidate beats its seed at all, with the
coin-flip line marked.](figures/dev_test_bars.png){#fig-devtest-bars width=100%}

One run shows the mechanism from the inside (@fig-devtest-case): a
Meta-Harness run on τ²-bench. Its own dev signal climbs the whole way, so to
the optimizer the run is a steady success. Re-scored on the sealed split, the
same candidates move the opposite direction — the true peak is one of the
earliest candidates, and everything after it is worse, ending below the seed.
The method locked onto its best candidate early, then spent the rest of its
budget walking away from it, because the dev signal kept rewarding the walk.

![One run from the inside. Dev score of each checkpoint (blue) vs. the
sealed-test score of the same candidates (orange), placed at the checkpoint
where each first appeared; dotted lines mark the seed's score on each split.
Dev and test disagree not just on how much was gained, but on which direction
the run was moving.](figures/dev_test_case.png){#fig-devtest-case width=88%}

We take this run apart item by item — and show that most of its dev climb is
selection noise, a mechanism decision analysis named the *optimizer's curse*
two decades ago — in a companion post:
[The Optimizer's Curse](../optimizers-curse/index.qmd).

## Calibrating lifts against the noise floor

We have leaned on the word *noise* throughout — here it is, measured. This
field is noisier than most: the worker is stochastic, the optimizer is stochastic, and so is
*scoring itself* — re-score a frozen, unchanged agent on the same sealed
split and a large share of items flip their verdict between repetitions. We
measured that floor directly, by re-scoring untouched seed agents under
identical conditions (@tbl-floor). The upshot: a single run's reported lift has to clear roughly six points
before it can be told apart from luck, and some reported optimization gains
fall below that.

| measured on a frozen, unchanged agent | value |
|---|---|
| items that flip verdict between re-scores | 20–40% |
| run-to-run sd of one test score (GPQA, haiku worker) | 0.021 |
| smallest lift a *single* run can show above 2σ noise | ~0.06 |

: The noise floor. Per-carrier, per-worker floors used later range roughly
0.010–0.034 in sd; the exact values are collected in the
benchmark-requirements section. {#tbl-floor}

This is not a quirk of our setup; the field is converging on the same
diagnosis (@tbl-related).

| study | setup | what they found |
|---|---|---|
| Gupta et al. [@nouniversalharness] | 30 harnesses × 12 model–problem pairs, 3M+ rollouts | once trials are repeated, no fixed harness is reliably superior |
| HarnessOpt-Bench [@harnessoptbench] | 40 configs, each run twice | median round-to-round range 0.07, worst 0.36; several ranges cross zero — the two rounds disagree on whether the optimizer helped at all |
| optimize_anything [@omni] | 3 optimizers, matched budget, 10 tasks | wins split 3–3–4; the winner flips task to task |

: Independent evaluations reaching the same conclusion — differences between
methods are often smaller than run-to-run variance. {#tbl-related}

The only honest response is repetition. Every cell in our grid is run as
several independent repeats, and lifts are reported against the measured floor
rather than a single lucky run. Repetition shrinks the bar a claim must clear
(@fig-noise) — but it never removes it.

![Repetition shrinks the required lift. Blue: the uncertainty of a reported
score as repeats increase. Orange: the smallest lift distinguishable from
noise at 2σ. The 1- and 3-repeat points are anchored by direct measurement; 5
is the √N extrapolation.](figures/noise_floor.png){#fig-noise width=88%}

When the budget runs out, the run is over, and what survives is everything the
comparison needs and nothing the method can spin: the candidate graph, the
checkpointed curve, the ledger, the full trace — and a floor that says how big
a lift has to be before it means anything. That leaves the constructive
question: what would it take to make these comparisons into a benchmark whose
rankings hold?

## Toward a reliable benchmark

We said at the top that this is not a benchmark release. Here is the
constructive version of that sentence. Every requirement below is
grounded in a failure we measured, not a hypothetical — and as far as we
can tell, no evaluation in this space (ours pre-dating this post
included, and the concurrent benchmarks [@evobench; @pastbench]) meets
more than a few of them.

1. **Report the noise floor as a first-class number.** Re-score an
   *unchanged* agent under the exact protocol, repeatedly, and print the
   sd next to every result table: ours is 0.021 (GPQA, haiku worker),
   0.010–0.017 (CharXiv, luna), and 0.022–0.034 (τ², luna — fewer test
   items, wider floor). Any effect inside ~2σ of that floor is a tier,
   not a rank. A headline gain reported without a floor
   — 16.6pp or otherwise — is not interpretable, because the reader
   cannot tell how many draws of pure noise it took to produce.

2. **Power the comparison before ranking it.** At sd ≈ 0.02 on a
   66-item test split, three scoring reps still leave per-cell standard
   errors of 0.01–0.02, while typical method effects are one to four
   points. The seeds-times-reps needed to resolve those effects at 2σ is
   a computable number; a benchmark should compute it and either pay it
   or report tiers. Our own grid, at current replication, resolves
   exactly one method separation (Meta-Harness on OSS-120B) — and we ran
   more repeats than is customary.

3. **Seal structurally, and resolve winners from the event record — not
   the run's say-so.** Test items must be unreachable through the
   method's interface, so overfitting the seal is impossible rather than
   discouraged. Just as important, and less obvious: the candidate a
   run's headline number refers to must be recovered from the evaluation
   events, not from the run's own summary. We found a bookkeeping
   off-by-one in checkpoint labeling that silently swapped which
   candidate a score was attributed to — the kind of bug that survives
   every plot and poisons a leaderboard invisibly. Attribution needs an
   audit path, which means the full event trace is a required artifact,
   not a nicety.

4. **Match and meter the budget, and report the curve.** A lift is a
   price, not a point: methods differ in where on the spend curve their
   gains arrive, and a fixed-budget snapshot reorders ranks as the
   budget moves — in an early thirteen-optimizer sweep of ours on
   BBH-hard, ranks kept reordering as the meter ran. Per-actor metering — optimizer
   thinking vs. worker rollouts — is what makes "at what cost" answerable
   at all.

5. **Stratify by headroom, because lift is a property of the pair.** A
   method that banks a clear lift where the worker is weak can do nothing
   measurable once the worker is strong on the tasks it is already good at
   (@fig-worker-axis) — and what lift remains at the frontier concentrates
   exactly where that worker's floor is lowest (the τ² points of
   @fig-anytime-meta). A pooled leaderboard number averages over the one
   variable that determines whether the method works at all. Report lift
   against seed floor, per worker tier; treat "does it still work at the
   frontier?" as a benchmark axis, not a footnote.

6. **Run validity controls like an adversary is coming.** A null-method
   arm (search that proposes nothing) to certify the floor — ours scored
   a lift of exactly zero, which is the only reason we trust the small
   positive lifts elsewhere. Jailed execution for methods that run
   LLM-authored code, because a benchmark whose harness can be
   reward-hacked measures compliance, not capability. And failure-rate
   reporting next to every Δ: a method that crashes a third of its runs
   has that fact laundered by a finished-runs-only table.

None of this is exotic; it is the ordinary machinery of measurement,
applied to a fast-moving field that has not yet installed it. Our
contribution, on reflection, is not a leaderboard — it is the instrument,
the ~80-cell corpus of fully-traced runs, the floor measurements, and the
two findings we believe survive every caveat in this post: **selection on
a noisy dev split takes back most of what optimization claims, and the gains
that survive concentrate where the model had headroom.** When a
benchmark in this space can meet the six requirements above, its rankings
will mean something. We intend MABench's next release to be judged
against exactly that list.
